query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal pre‐treatment that induces surface segregation and enrichment of copper in a near‐equiatomic multi‐principal-element catalyst will enhance low‐temperature oxidation activity, improve resistance to common exhaust poisons (H2O, NO), and extend lifetime durability without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with a homogeneous distribution of elements including copper, nickel, and minimal platinum-group metals.
generation.intervention: Apply a mild thermal oxidation/reduction cycling pre‐treatment designed to drive selective copper segregation to the catalyst surface.
generation.conditions: Tested under transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions (oxidation below 150 °C), in the presence of typical poisoning species such as H2O and NO, and aged under accelerated aging protocols simulating a full vehicle lifetime.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface enrichment of copper that forms active Cu–O species while altering surface adsorption sites.
generation.mechanism: The enriched copper surface facilitates lower activation energy pathways for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation and modifies adsorption properties to resist poisoning by H2O and NO. The resulting Cu‐rich layer also promotes self-healing or slower degradation under thermal cycling and mileage-related stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is expected to lower the light-off temperature of the catalyst (e.g., below 150 °C), improve resistance toward poisoning (maintaining performance in the presence of H2O and NO), and slow degradation over long-term aging compared to the unmodified catalyst.
generation.baseline: An unmodified near‐equiatomic multi‐principal-element catalyst that exhibits higher activation temperatures, more severe poisoning effects, and accelerated degradation under simulated real-driving and aging conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits should be observable under laboratory conditions that closely simulate real exhaust gases and transient operation as well as under accelerated aging protocols representative of a vehicle’s lifetime mileage. Outside these conditions, the effects and durability of the Cu‐rich surface may not be as pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal thermal treatment parameters required for effective and durable Cu surface segregation and how stable the resulting enriched layer remains under prolonged cycling and real-world exhaust fluctuations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set receives the controlled thermal oxidation/reduction pre‐treatment to induce Cu segregation, while the control remains unmodified. Subject both to standardized catalytic testing under low-temperature (below 150 °C) exhaust conditions containing H2O and NO. Perform accelerated aging tests that simulate vehicle lifetime mileage. Use surface analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM–EDS) before and after aging to verify Cu enrichment and stability.
measurements: Light-off temperature (temperature at which 50% conversion is achieved) for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
Activity retention in the presence of poisoning species (H2O, NO)
Durability metrics (conversion rates and surface composition changes) before and after aging
Surface composition and morphology assessment (via XPS and SEM–EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be considered falsified if the pre-treated catalysts do not show a statistically significant reduction in light-off temperature, fail to demonstrate improved performance in the presence of H2O and NO compared to the control, or exhibit similar or worse degradation in activity and surface composition after aging.
